newsitem.title: USA: Dow shuffles 100-year old blue-chip average.
newsitem.headline: Dow shuffles 100-year old blue-chip average.

text.p: The most exclusive club on Wall Street is getting some new members -- and letting some old ones go.

For the first time in nearly six years, the Dow Jones industrial average of 30 blue-chip stocks, the most closely followed stock index in the world, will shuffle its membership in order to more closely reflect the changing economy.
Joining the roster are healthcare products company Johnson & Johnson, top U.S. retailer Wal-Mart Stores Inc., insurance company Travelers Group Inc., and computer-maker Hewlett-Packard Co..
Leaving the Dow's ranks are Bethlehem Steel Corp., Westinghouse Electric Corp., Texaco Inc. and retailer Woolworth Corp..

"Nowadays, technological innovation and services of all types are major propellants of the U.S. economy," said Paul Steiger, managing editor of the Wall Street Journal, which is published by Dow Jones & Co.
The Dow index marked its 100th anniversaary in 1996, but dates back to 1884 when Charles Dow, a co-founder of Dow Jones produced a stock market average of 11 stocks.
Wall Street analysts supported the moves, saying the benchmark average was long in need of change.
"This will help the Dow immensely," said Yale Hirsch, a veteran Dow watcher who runs the Hirsch Organization.

"Bethlehem Steel and Woolworth are just no longer vibrant companies representative of American industry. Travelers and Hewlett-Packard are just more important," Charles Lemonides, managing director of Sterling Advisors, a division of Gruntal & Co.

The removal of Texaco from the Dow reflects the growing importance of service and techonology companies, such as Hewlett-Packard, in the overall economy. Two other major oil companies, Exxon Corp. and Chevron Corp. remain in the Dow.
"It seemed a little strange to have 10 percent of the companies in the DJIA as oil companies", said Fred Leuffer, oil analyst at Bear Stearns.
The removal of Westinghouse is based on its decision to spin off its industrial operations later this year and focus on its broadcasting business, which includes the CBS network.

Lemonides said a small market capitalization probably played a factor in the decision to eliminate the other companies. Bethlehem Steel has a market capitalization of about $1 billion, he said, compared with about $80 billion for pharmaceutical giant Johnson & Johnson.
The last time that the components of the venerable average, which celebrated its 100th birthday in 1996, were changed was in May 1991.

Heavy equipment maker Caterpillar Inc., Walt Disney Co. and bank J.P. Morgan & Co. Inc. were added to the average then. Truck maker Navistar International, steel and energy firm USX Corp. and insurance firm Primerica Corp. were dropped.
In a twist, Primerica has bought itself back into the Dow. It bought Hartford-based insurance company Travelers Inc. at the end of 1993 and adopted the Travelers name.
Analysts said the changes could give a boost to the stocks added to the average but stressed that it would be short-term.

"The change is likely to create a slight upward bias for simple reason that the companies added will be widely owned and widely bought by investing institutions," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albany.

But "the question I keep asking myself is 'Why are we limited to (NYSE) listed stocks and why are we not looking at Intel and Microsoft?' Certainly, semiconductors and software are under-represented in the Dow," he said. Both Microsoft Corp. and Intel Corp. are listed on Nasdaq.
